claim: Video games are one of the most popular forms of entertainment, with 25% of the European population reporting playing video games weekly.
source: In Europe, 25% of the population report playing video games weekly, and especially young adults spend much time in these 'virtual worlds' (IPSOS MediaCT, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to IPSOS MediaCT, 2012.

claim: Many popular video games contain high levels of violent imagery, with killing or hurting other characters being deeply engrained in gameplay.
source: Many popular games contain high levels of violent imagery, with the killing or hurting of other characters being deeply engrained in the gameplay (Gentile et al., 2004; Krantz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gentile et al., 2004 and Krantz et al., 2017.

claim: According to the general aggression model, violent video games should decrease players' empathy for the pain of others by desensitizing them to both virtual and real violence.
source: According to the influential general aggression model (Bushman and Anderson, 2002), VVGs should decrease the players' empathy for the pain of others by desensitizing them to both virtual and real violence.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bushman and Anderson, 2002, which describes the general aggression model.

claim: Desensitizing effects of violent video games should be reflected by decreased activity in brain areas underpinning empathy, such as the anterior insula and anterior midcingulate cortex.
source: Such desensitizing effects should in turn be reflected by decreased activity in brain areas underpinning empathy, such as the anterior insula (AI) and the anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) (Lamm et al., 2011; Lamm et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lamm et al., 2011 and Lamm et al., 2019, which identify brain areas underpinning empathy.

claim: Some studies found that playing violent video games leads to emotional desensitization on the behavioral and neural level.
source: While some studies found that playing VVGs leads to emotional desensitization on the behavioral and neural level (Arriaga et al., 2011; Bartholow et al., 2006; Carnagey et al., 2007; Engelhardt et al., 2011; Staude-Müller et al., 2008), other studies failed to reveal such effects (Gao et al., 2017; Kühn et al., 2018; Szycik et al., 2017a; Szycik et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies reporting desensitization effects.

claim: Other studies failed to reveal desensitization effects of violent video games on the behavioral and neural level.
source: While some studies found that playing VVGs leads to emotional desensitization on the behavioral and neural level (Arriaga et al., 2011; Bartholow et al., 2006; Carnagey et al., 2007; Engelhardt et al., 2011; Staude-Müller et al., 2008), other studies failed to reveal such effects (Gao et al., 2017; Kühn et al., 2018; Szycik et al., 2017a; Szycik et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies that did not find desensitization effects.

claim: Several meta-analyses suggest that violent video games exert small, yet consistent adverse effects on aggression and empathy.
source: Several meta-analyses suggest that VVGs exert small, yet consistent adverse effects on aggression and empathy (Anderson et al., 2010; Calvert et al., 2017; Greitemeyer and Mügge, 2014; Mathur and VanderWeele, 2019; Prescott et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple meta-analyses.

claim: Some researchers contest meta-analysis results on violent video game effects, claiming that results are a product of selective reporting and biased analyses.
source: Other researchers contest these results, claiming that results are a product of selective reporting and biased analyses (Ferguson and Kilburn, 2010; Hilgard et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferguson and Kilburn, 2010 and Hilgard et al., 2017b.

claim: Many studies on violent video games have been quasi-experimental in nature, comparing empathic responses of habitual violent video game players with those without violent video game experience.
source: Many studies have been quasi-experimental in nature, comparing the empathic responses of participants who habitually play VVGs with those of participants without VVG experience (Bartholow et al., 2005; Bartholow et al., 2006; Gentile et al., 2016; Krahé et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple quasi-experimental studies.

claim: Quasi-experimental designs provide limited information on the direction of the causal link between violent video games and decreased empathy.
source: Such designs provide limited information on the direction of the causal link between VVGs and decreased empathy.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the limitations of quasi-experimental designs described in the manuscript.

claim: Existing experimental studies on violent video games have nearly always used violent video games as an experimental manipulation shortly before measuring outcomes of interest.
source: The existing experimental studies have nearly always used VVGs as an experimental manipulation shortly before measuring the outcomes of interest (Arriaga et al., 2011; Bushman and Anderson, 2009; Carnagey et al., 2007; Engelhardt et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2013; Staude-Müller et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies.

claim: Studies using violent video games as an experimental manipulation shortly before measuring outcomes consistently report evidence for a desensitizing effect of violent games.
source: While these studies consistently report evidence for a desensitizing effect of violent games, they cannot disentangle the immediate effects of VVG play from those that have a persistent, long-term impact on individuals.
evidence: The claim is based on a summary of findings from the cited experimental studies.

claim: Short-term experimental studies on violent video games cannot disentangle immediate effects from persistent, long-term impacts on individuals.
source: While these studies consistently report evidence for a desensitizing effect of violent games, they cannot disentangle the immediate effects of VVG play from those that have a persistent, long-term impact on individuals.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of short-term experimental designs.

claim: Kühn et al., 2018 found no significant effects of violent video games on empathy and its neural correlates.
source: One first such study was conducted by Kühn et al., 2018, who found no significant effects of VVGs on empathy and its neural correlates.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kühn et al., 2018.

claim: The study by Kühn et al., 2018 used very dissimilar games in the experimental group versus the control group, restricting comparability of the two conditions.
source: First, the researchers used very dissimilar games in the experimental group versus the control group, restricting the comparability of the two conditions.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the methodology of Kühn et al., 2018.

claim: The study by Kühn et al., 2018 did not control the degree to which participants actually played the game.
source: Second, while the participants of the experimental group were asked to play the violent game Grand Theft Auto V (Rockstar Studios) for 30 min per day over 2 months, the authors did not control the degree to which participants actually played the game.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the methodology of Kühn et al., 2018.

claim: The study by Kühn et al., 2018 did not control that participants actually committed violent acts within the game.
source: Third, the authors did not control that participants actually committed violent acts within the game, as the game offers a large amount of gameplay without violent content.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the methodology of Kühn et al., 2018.

claim: The study by Kühn et al., 2018 did not report equivalence tests or Bayesian hypothesis tests to support claims of absence of violent video game effects.
source: Fourth, the absence of significant results was interpreted as evidence for the absence of VVG effects. However, the authors did not report the results of equivalence tests (Lakens et al., 2018) or Bayesian hypothesis tests (Keysers et al., 2020) that would support such claims conclusively (Hilgard et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the statistical analysis in Kühn et al., 2018, supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: Eighty-nine male participants with little to no prior violent video game experience participated in the current study.
source: Eighty-nine male participants with little to no prior VVG experience repeatedly played a modified version of Grand Theft Auto V over the course of 2 weeks.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: Participants in the experimental group played a highly violent version of Grand Theft Auto V and were tasked to kill as many other characters as possible.
source: Participants in the experimental group played a highly violent version of the game and were tasked to kill as many other characters as possible.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: Participants in the control group played a version of Grand Theft Auto V from which all violent content was removed and were asked to perform a non-violent task (taking photographs of other characters).
source: Participants of the control group played a version of the same game from which all violent content was removed, and were asked to perform a non-violent task (taking photographs of other characters).
evidence: This is a description of the control condition.

claim: Before and after the gaming period, participants completed a functional magnetic resonance imaging session during which behavioral and neural correlates of empathy for pain and emotional reactivity to violent images were measured.
source: Before and after this gaming period, participants completed a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) session during which we measured the behavioral and neural correlates of empathy for pain and emotional reactivity to violent images (see Figure 1 and Methods: Experimental fMRI sessions for details).
evidence: This is a description of the study design and measurements.

claim: Bayesian hypothesis tests were used to assess whether there were negative effects of violent video games on participants' empathic behavior and neural responses.
source: We used Bayesian hypothesis tests to assess whether there were negative effects of VVGs on participants' empathic behavior and neural responses.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis approach.

claim: A Bayes factor greater than 3 was reported as evidence for the alternative hypothesis.
source: We followed the convention to report a BF>3 as evidence for the alternative hypothesis, a BF<1/3 as evidence for the null hypothesis, and a BF in the interval [1/3, 3] as inconclusive evidence for either hypothesis (Kass and Raftery, 1995; Keysers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical interpretation framework, supported by citations.

claim: A Bayes factor less than 1/3 was reported as evidence for the null hypothesis.
source: We followed the convention to report a BF>3 as evidence for the alternative hypothesis, a BF<1/3 as evidence for the null hypothesis, and a BF in the interval [1/3, 3] as inconclusive evidence for either hypothesis (Kass and Raftery, 1995; Keysers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical interpretation framework, supported by citations.

claim: A Bayes factor in the interval [1/3, 3] was reported as inconclusive evidence for either hypothesis.
source: We followed the convention to report a BF>3 as evidence for the alternative hypothesis, a BF<1/3 as evidence for the null hypothesis, and a BF in the interval [1/3, 3] as inconclusive evidence for either hypothesis (Kass and Raftery, 1995; Keysers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical interpretation framework, supported by citations.

claim: Participants of the experimental group killed an average of 2844.7 characters during the gaming sessions.
source: On average, participants of the experimental group killed 2844.7 characters (SD = 993.9, median = 2820, minimum = 441, maximum = 6815).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the gaming behavior data.

claim: Participants of the control group took an average of 3055.3 pictures of other characters during the gaming sessions.
source: Participants of the control group took an average of 3055.3 pictures of other characters (SD = 1307.5, median = 3026, minimum = 441, maximum = 6815).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the gaming behavior data.

claim: Each participant of the experimental group was exposed to a substantial number of violent acts in the video game.
source: Thus, as was the aim of our experimental design, each participant of the experimental group was exposed to a substantial number of violent acts in the video game.
evidence: This is an inference based on the descriptive statistics of gaming behavior.

claim: Painful stimuli led to increased painfulness ratings compared to non-painful stimuli, with very strong evidence (BF>100).
source: As a manipulation check, we first tested whether painful stimuli led to increased painfulness and unpleasantness ratings, compared to non-painful stimuli. For both kinds of ratings, this test revealed very strong evidence (BF>100) for an effect of intensity, indicating that our paradigm was able to induce empathic responses in participants (see Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the empathy-for-pain task, with reference to Figure 2A and B.

claim: Painful stimuli led to increased unpleasantness ratings compared to non-painful stimuli, with very strong evidence (BF>100).
source: As a manipulation check, we first tested whether painful stimuli led to increased painfulness and unpleasantness ratings, compared to non-painful stimuli. For both kinds of ratings, this test revealed very strong evidence (BF>100) for an effect of intensity, indicating that our paradigm was able to induce empathic responses in participants (see Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the empathy-for-pain task, with reference to Figure 2A and B.

claim: The empathy-for-pain paradigm was able to induce empathic responses in participants.
source: For both kinds of ratings, this test revealed very strong evidence (BF>100) for an effect of intensity, indicating that our paradigm was able to induce empathic responses in participants (see Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical results showing effects of stimulus intensity.

claim: The posterior mean of the regression parameter β of the factor Intensity was 27.86 for painfulness ratings.
source: The posterior mean of the regression parameter β of the factor Intensity was 27.86 for painfulness ratings, and 17.48 for unpleasantness ratings.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian regression model.

claim: The posterior mean of the regression parameter β of the factor Intensity was 17.48 for unpleasantness ratings.
source: The posterior mean of the regression parameter β of the factor Intensity was 27.86 for painfulness ratings, and 17.48 for unpleasantness ratings.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian regression model.

claim: The average difference in painfulness ratings between painful and non-painful stimuli was 55.72 points on the 100-point visual analog scale.
source: Given our used factor coding, this means that the average difference in ratings between painful and non-painful stimuli was 2*27.86=55.72 points of the 100-point VAS for painfulness ratings, and 2*17.48=34.96 points for unpleasantness ratings.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the regression parameter estimate.

claim: The average difference in unpleasantness ratings between painful and non-painful stimuli was 34.96 points on the 100-point visual analog scale.
source: Given our used factor coding, this means that the average difference in ratings between painful and non-painful stimuli was 2*27.86=55.72 points of the 100-point VAS for painfulness ratings, and 2*17.48=34.96 points for unpleasantness ratings.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the regression parameter estimate.

claim: There is evidence for the absence of a violent video game effect on painfulness ratings (BF = 0.324).
source: We found evidence for the absence of a VVG effect on the painfulness ratings. Comparing a model where the fixed effect of Group*Time*Intensity could be negative to a model where the effect was set to zero resulted in a BF of 0.324.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian hypothesis test.

claim: The observed painfulness ratings were about 3.1 times more likely under the null hypothesis of no violent video game effect than under the alternative hypothesis.
source: This means that the observed ratings were about 3.1 times more likely under the null hypothesis of no VVG effect than under the alternative hypothesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayes factor result.

claim: The posterior mean of β for the interaction Group*Session*Intensity was –0.78 for painfulness ratings.
source: When estimated without restrictions, the posterior mean of β for the interaction Group*Session*Intensity was –0.78.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian regression model.

claim: For unpleasantness ratings, evidence for absence of a violent video game effect was substantial (BF = 0.130).
source: For the unpleasantness ratings, evidence for absence of a VVG effect was substantial. With a BF of 0.130, the observed data were about 7.7 times more likely under the null hypothesis of no VVG effect than under the alternative hypothesis.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian hypothesis test.

claim: The observed unpleasantness ratings were about 7.7 times more likely under the null hypothesis of no violent video game effect than under the alternative hypothesis.
source: With a BF of 0.130, the observed data were about 7.7 times more likely under the null hypothesis of no VVG effect than under the alternative hypothesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayes factor result.

claim: The posterior mean of β for the interaction Group*Session*Intensity was –0.45 for unpleasantness ratings.
source: The posterior mean of β for the interaction Group*Session*Intensity was –0.45.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian regression model.

claim: The behavioral data suggest that violent video game play as implemented in this study has no effect on either type of empathy rating.
source: In summary, the behavioral data suggest that VVG play as implemented in this study has no effect on either type of empathy rating.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the statistical results from the empathy-for-pain task.

claim: Participants experienced more unpleasantness while observing violent pictures compared to neutral pictures, with very strong evidence (BF>100).
source: As a manipulation check, we first tested whether participants experienced more unpleasantness in the emotional reactivity task while observing violent pictures compared to neutral pictures. We found very strong evidence (BF>100) for this hypothesis, indicating that our paradigm was successful in inducing unpleasantness by violent imagery.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the emotional reactivity task.

claim: The emotional reactivity paradigm was successful in inducing unpleasantness by violent imagery.
source: We found very strong evidence (BF>100) for this hypothesis, indicating that our paradigm was successful in inducing unpleasantness by violent imagery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical results showing effects of violent content.

claim: The posterior mean of the regression parameter β of the factor Content was 37.08 for unpleasantness ratings in the emotional reactivity task.
source: The posterior mean of the regression parameter β of the factor Content was 37.08.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian regression model.

claim: The average difference in unpleasantness ratings between violent and neutral stimuli was 74.16 points on the 100-point visual analog scale in the emotional reactivity task.
source: This means that the average difference in ratings between violent and neutral stimuli was 74.16 points of the 100-point VAS.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the regression parameter estimate.

claim: There is substantial evidence for the absence of a desensitizing violent video game effect on emotional reactivity (BF = 0.151 for Group*Content interaction).
source: Further, we found substantial evidence for the absence of a desensitizing VVG effect. Comparing a model where the fixed effect of Group*Content could be negative to a model where the effect was set to zero resulted in a BF of 0.151.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian hypothesis test.

claim: Participants of the violent game group did not show a decreased emotional response toward depictions of real and game violence.
source: Thus, participants of the violent game group did not show a decreased emotional response toward depictions of real and game violence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the statistical results from the emotional reactivity task.

claim: There was no desensitizing effect of violent video games that was specific to depictions of game violence (BF = 0.094 for Group*Content*Context interaction).
source: Moreover, testing the fixed effect of Group*Content*Context resulted in a BF of 0.094, indicating that there was also no desensitizing effect that was specific to depictions of game violence.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian hypothesis test.

claim: The behavioral data suggest that playing the violent video game did not emotionally desensitize participants toward violent images.
source: In summary, the behavioral data suggest that playing the VVG did not emotionally desensitize participants toward violent images.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the statistical results from the emotional reactivity task.

claim: Whole-brain analysis of the first fMRI session revealed significant clusters in the anterior midcingulate cortex and bilateral anterior insula for the contrast [Other Pain – Other No Pain].
source: This revealed significant clusters in our a priori defined brain areas of interest, aMCC and bilateral AI, as well as in other areas, including the left supramarginal gyrus and the right angular gyrus (see Figure 3A, and Appendix 3 for detailed results).
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Whole-brain analysis of the first fMRI session revealed significant clusters in the left supramarginal gyrus and right angular gyrus for the contrast [Other Pain – Other No Pain].
source: This revealed significant clusters in our a priori defined brain areas of interest, aMCC and bilateral AI, as well as in other areas, including the left supramarginal gyrus and the right angular gyrus (see Figure 3A, and Appendix 3 for detailed results).
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: For responses in the Cue phase of the empathy-for-pain task, there is weak to moderate evidence for the absence of an effect of playing the violent video game on brain activity (BFaMCC = 0.402; BFleft AI = 0.547; BFright AI = 0.190).
source: For responses in the Cue phase (where participants were informed whether the other person would receive a painful or a non-painful stimulus), we obtained the following BFs: BFaMCC = 0.402; BFleft AI = 0.547; BFright AI = 0.190.
evidence: These are statistical results from the Bayesian hypothesis tests on fMRI data.

claim: For responses in the Stimulation phase of the empathy-for-pain task, there is weak to moderate evidence for the absence of an effect of playing the violent video game on brain activity (BFaMCC = 0.176; BFleft AI = 0.143; BFright AI = 0.434).
source: For responses in the Stimulation phase (where participants observed the other person receiving the stimulus), we obtained the following BFs: BFaMCC = 0.176; BFleft AI = 0.143; BFright AI = 0.434.
evidence: These are statistical results from the Bayesian hypothesis tests on fMRI data.

claim: There is weak to moderate evidence for the absence of an effect of playing the violent video game on participants' brain activity while they observed another person in pain.
source: In summary, we found weak to moderate evidence for the absence of an effect of playing the VVG on participants' brain activity while they observed another person in pain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the statistical results from the fMRI analysis of the empathy-for-pain task.

claim: Whole-brain analysis revealed significant clusters in the bilateral amygdala for the contrast [Violent – Neutral] in the emotional reactivity task.
source: This revealed significant clusters in one of our a priori areas of interest, the bilateral amygdala, as well as several other regions, such as the bilateral fusiform gyrus and the bilateral precentral gyrus (see Figure 3B and Appendix 3 for detailed results).
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Whole-brain analysis revealed significant clusters in the bilateral fusiform gyrus and bilateral precentral gyrus for the contrast [Violent – Neutral] in the emotional reactivity task.
source: This revealed significant clusters in one of our a priori areas of interest, the bilateral amygdala, as well as several other regions, such as the bilateral fusiform gyrus and the bilateral precentral gyrus (see Figure 3B and Appendix 3 for detailed results).
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: No significant clusters were found in the anterior midcingulate cortex or bilateral anterior insula for the contrast [Violent – Neutral] in the emotional reactivity task.
source: However, we found no significant clusters in the other brain ROIs, the aMCC or the bilateral AI.
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain fMRI analysis.

claim: For the left amygdala, there is evidence for the absence of an effect of Group*Content (BF = 0.324).
source: First, we compared a model where the fixed effect of Group*Content could be negative to a model where the effect was set to zero. This resulted in a BF of 0.324 for the left amygdala, and a BF of 0.338 for the right amygdala, indicating absence of an effect in both ROIs.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian hypothesis test on fMRI data.

claim: For the right amygdala, there is evidence for the absence of an effect of Group*Content (BF = 0.338).
source: First, we compared a model where the fixed effect of Group*Content could be negative to a model where the effect was set to zero. This resulted in a BF of 0.324 for the left amygdala, and a BF of 0.338 for the right amygdala, indicating absence of an effect in both ROIs.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian hypothesis test on fMRI data.

claim: For the left amygdala, there is evidence for the absence of an effect of Group*Content*Context (BF = 0.205).
source: Next, we tested the fixed effect of Group*Content*Context. With a BF of 0.205 for the left amygdala, and 0.163 for the right amygdala, this analysis also indicated the absence of an effect.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian hypothesis test on fMRI data.

claim: For the right amygdala, there is evidence for the absence of an effect of Group*Content*Context (BF = 0.163).
source: Next, we tested the fixed effect of Group*Content*Context. With a BF of 0.205 for the left amygdala, and 0.163 for the right amygdala, this analysis also indicated the absence of an effect.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Bayesian hypothesis test on fMRI data.

claim: The fMRI data suggest that playing the violent video game did not lead to a dampened brain response to images of violence in neither real nor gaming contexts.
source: In summary, the data suggest that playing the VVG did not lead to a dampened brain response to images of violence in neither real nor gaming contexts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the statistical results from the fMRI analysis of the emotional reactivity task.

claim: For all subdimensions of the Questionnaire for Cognitive and Affective Empathy, Bayesian t-tests provided moderate to substantial evidence for the hypothesis that there is no difference in trait empathy between the experimental sample and the control sample (BF<1/3).
source: For all subdimensions, Bayesian t-tests provided moderate to substantial evidence for the hypothesis that there is no difference between the two groups (BF<1/3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the post hoc analysis comparing trait empathy levels.

claim: The inclusion criterion of minimal violent video game exposure did not result in a preselection of individuals with extraordinarily high levels of empathy.
source: Thus, our exploratory analysis suggests that our inclusion criterion of minimal VVG exposure did not result in a preselection of individuals with extraordinarily high levels of empathy.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the statistical results from the trait empathy comparison.

claim: The test-retest reliability of behavioral measures of empathy (painfulness ratings) was high (ρ=0.768, 95% credible interval = [0.613, 0.879]).
source: We found that the test-retest reliability of our behavioral measures of empathy (i.e. participants' ratings) was high to very high (painfulness ratings: ρ=0.768, 95% credible interval = [0.613, 0.879]; unpleasantness ratings: ρ=0.905, 95% credible interval = [0.813, 0.967]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the test-retest reliability analysis.

claim: The test-retest reliability of behavioral measures of empathy (unpleasantness ratings) was very high (ρ=0.905, 95% credible interval = [0.813, 0.967]).
source: We found that the test-retest reliability of our behavioral measures of empathy (i.e. participants' ratings) was high to very high (painfulness ratings: ρ=0.768, 95% credible interval = [0.613, 0.879]; unpleasantness ratings: ρ=0.905, 95% credible interval = [0.813, 0.967]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the test-retest reliability analysis.

claim: Very low test-retest reliability was observed for neural measurements of empathy in the anterior midcingulate cortex (ρ=–0.013, 95% credible interval = [–0.420, 0.402]).
source: However, we observed very low test-retest reliability for our neural measurements of empathy (aMCC signal: ρ=–0.013, 95% credible interval = [–0.420, 0.402]; left AI signal, ρ=–0.001, 95% credible interval = [–0.423, 0.414]; right AI signal, ρ=0.027, 95% credible interval = [–0.377, 0.416]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the test-retest reliability analysis.

claim: Very low test-retest reliability was observed for neural measurements of empathy in the left anterior insula (ρ=–0.001, 95% credible interval = [–0.423, 0.414]).
source: However, we observed very low test-retest reliability for our neural measurements of empathy (aMCC signal: ρ=–0.013, 95% credible interval = [–0.420, 0.402]; left AI signal, ρ=–0.001, 95% credible interval = [–0.423, 0.414]; right AI signal, ρ=0.027, 95% credible interval = [–0.377, 0.416]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the test-retest reliability analysis.

claim: Very low test-retest reliability was observed for neural measurements of empathy in the right anterior insula (ρ=0.027, 95% credible interval = [–0.377, 0.416]).
source: However, we observed very low test-retest reliability for our neural measurements of empathy (aMCC signal: ρ=–0.013, 95% credible interval = [–0.420, 0.402]; left AI signal, ρ=–0.001, 95% credible interval = [–0.423, 0.414]; right AI signal, ρ=0.027, 95% credible interval = [–0.377, 0.416]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the test-retest reliability analysis.

claim: The behavioral analyses were well enough powered to differentiate between the absence and presence of a medium-to-small effect of d=0.3.
source: In summary, the simulation experiment suggested that our behavioral analyses, for which test-retest reliabilities were high, were well enough powered to differentiate between the absence and presence of a medium-to-small effect of d=0.3.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Bayesian design analysis simulation.

claim: The effect size d=0.3 is smaller than the lower bound of effect size estimates reported in the meta-analysis of Anderson et al., 2010, which was d=0.345.
source: Note that this effect size is smaller than the lower bound of effect size estimates reported in the meta-analysis of Anderson et al., 2010, which was d=0.345.
evidence: This is a comparison of effect sizes, with a citation to Anderson et al., 2010.

claim: For smaller effects such as d=0.2, the a priori power of the behavioral analyses was not optimal.
source: For smaller effects, such as d=0.2, the a priori power of our behavioral analyses was not optimal, as it would have been likely that we would have obtained an inconclusive result (1/3<BF<3) even in the presence of a true effect of that size.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Bayesian design analysis simulation.

claim: Given that evidence for the null hypothesis (BF<1/3) was obtained in all relevant Bayes factor tests on behavioral data, the results speak strongly against the presence of an effect of d=0.2.
source: However, given that we obtained evidence for the null hypothesis (BF<1/3) in all relevant BF tests on our behavioral data, our results speak strongly against the presence of such an effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of the Bayesian design analysis and the actual statistical results.

claim: Given the low correlation between repeated measurements (test-retest reliability), the Bayesian power of the fMRI analyses should be regarded as low.
source: Regarding our neural analyses, given the low correlation between repeated measurements (i.e. test-retest reliability), the Bayesian power of our fMRI analyses should be regarded as low.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the test-retest reliability results and the Bayesian design analysis.

claim: The fMRI results, taken alone, would not be considered convincing evidence against the presence of a violent video game effect.
source: Taken alone, we would not consider them convincing evidence against the presence of a VVG effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results in light of the low statistical power.

claim: Together with the behavioral results, the fMRI results suggest that violent video game effects, if they exist, can be expected to be very small.
source: However, together with our behavioral results, they suggest that VVG effects, if they exist, can be expected to be very small.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of behavioral and fMRI results.

claim: For behavioral measures, cross-task correlations between empathy for pain and emotional reactivity were substantial (r=0.227–0.280, with all credible intervals not covering zero).
source: We can observe that for our behavioral measures, cross-task correlations were substantial (r=0.227 –0.280, with all credible intervals not covering zero).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cross-task correlation analysis.

claim: No substantial cross-task correlations were observed for neural measures of empathy and emotional reactivity.
source: However, we could observe no substantial cross-task correlations for our neural measures, or across neural and behavioral indicators.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cross-task correlation analysis.

claim: No substantial cross-task correlations were observed across neural and behavioral indicators of empathy and emotional reactivity.
source: However, we could observe no substantial cross-task correlations for our neural measures, or across neural and behavioral indicators.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cross-task correlation analysis.

claim: Participants who repeatedly played a highly violent game for 7 hours over the course of 2 weeks did not show decreased empathy for another person's pain.
source: We found that participants who repeatedly played a highly violent game for 7 hr over the course of 2 weeks did not show decreased empathy for another person's pain or decreased responses to violent imagery.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the behavioral and neural data.

claim: Participants who repeatedly played a highly violent game for 7 hours over the course of 2 weeks did not show decreased responses to violent imagery.
source: We found that participants who repeatedly played a highly violent game for 7 hr over the course of 2 weeks did not show decreased empathy for another person's pain or decreased responses to violent imagery.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the behavioral and neural data.

claim: The findings contrast with several earlier studies that found a negative relationship between playing violent video games and empathic responses to violence.
source: Our findings contrast with several earlier studies that found a negative relationship between playing VVGs and empathic responses to violence.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previous literature.

claim: The majority of earlier studies finding negative relationships between violent video games and empathy were quasi-experimental in nature and provide only limited evidence for a putative causal effect.
source: Importantly, the majority of these studies were quasi-experimental in nature, and therefore provide only limited evidence for a putative causal effect of violent gaming (Bartholow et al., 2005; Bartholow et al., 2006; Gentile et al., 2016; Krahé et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: The few experimental studies that exist on violent video game effects implemented designs investigating short-term carryover effects.
source: Moreover, the few experimental studies that exist implemented designs investigating short-term carryover effects, as they had exposed participants to virtual violence rather immediately before measurements of their outcome variables of interest (Arriaga et al., 2011; Bushman and Anderson, 2009; Carnagey et al., 2007; Engelhardt et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2013; Staude-Müller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Together with the study of Kühn et al., 2018, the current study is one of the first to investigate persistent effects of violent video games in participants without prior experience with them.
source: Together with the study of Kühn et al., 2018, our study is one of the first to investigate persistent effects of VVGs in participants without prior experience with them, enabling a clear assessment of the causality of VVG effects.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study design, with a citation to Kühn et al., 2018.

claim: The current study was designed to address several limitations of the study of Kühn et al., 2018.
source: Importantly, our study was designed to address several limitations of the study of Kühn et al.: We strictly controlled the amount of virtual violence actually experienced by participants, and used a non-violent version of the same game in the control condition; moreover, we applied a Bayesian analytical approach, which, together with our comparatively large sample size, enabled us from the outset to distinguish 'absence of evidence' from 'evidence of absence' of VVG effects.
evidence: This is a description of the study design improvements over previous work.

claim: The study strictly controlled the amount of virtual violence actually experienced by participants.
source: We strictly controlled the amount of virtual violence actually experienced by participants, and used a non-violent version of the same game in the control condition
evidence: This is a description of a key design feature of the study.

claim: The study used a non-violent version of the same game in the control condition.
source: We strictly controlled the amount of virtual violence actually experienced by participants, and used a non-violent version of the same game in the control condition
evidence: This is a description of a key design feature of the study.

claim: The study applied a Bayesian analytical approach, which enabled distinguishing 'absence of evidence' from 'evidence of absence' of violent video game effects.
source: moreover, we applied a Bayesian analytical approach, which, together with our comparatively large sample size, enabled us from the outset to distinguish 'absence of evidence' from 'evidence of absence' of VVG effects.
evidence: This is a description of the analytical approach and its advantages.

claim: The Bayesian analytical approach yields consistent evidence from both behavioral and neural data that violent video games, to the extent and characteristics played in the interventional design, are not causally responsible for a persistent lack of empathy or emotional desensitization to violence.
source: This approach yields consistent evidence from both behavioral and neural data that VVGs, to the extent and characteristics played in our interventional design, are not causally responsible for a persistent lack of empathy or emotional desensitization to violence.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the Bayesian analyses of behavioral and neural data.

claim: The overall exposure to virtual violence in the study was very low when compared to the amount that is possible in the everyday life of typical violent video game players.
source: However, the overall exposure to virtual violence was still very low when compared to the amount that is possible in the everyday life of typical VVG players.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: During the experiment, participants played for 7 hours over the course of 2 weeks, while habitual gamers can play an average of 16 hours in the same time frame.
source: During our experiment, participants played for 7 hr over the course of 2 weeks. However, habitual gamers can play an average of 16 hr in the same time frame (Clement, 2021; Statista Research Department, 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison of the experimental exposure to typical gaming behavior, supported by citations.

claim: The results cannot preclude that longer and more intense exposure to violent video games could have negative causal effects on empathy.
source: Our results cannot preclude that longer and more intense exposure to VVGs could have negative causal effects on empathy.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study's generalizability.

claim: Adolescents and children as well as persons with specific neuropsychiatric traits might be especially susceptible to long-term changes due to increased brain plasticity.
source: In particular, adolescents and children as well as persons with specific neuropsychiatric traits might be especially susceptible to long-term changes due to increased brain plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential vulnerable populations, based on knowledge about brain plasticity.

claim: The results provide an important perspective on the size of violent video game effects that could realistically be expected in experimental research.
source: We thus believe that our results provide an important perspective on the size of VVG effects that could realistically be expected in experimental research.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the findings.

claim: The sample was restricted to young adult males who had minimal prior exposure to violent video games to increase experimental control.
source: To increase experimental control, we restricted our sample to young adult males who had minimal prior exposure to VVGs.
evidence: This is a description of the sample selection criteria.

claim: It is possible that due to the strict preselection criterion, the sample was drawn from a subpopulation that is particularly resistant to desensitization.
source: It is possible that, due to this strict preselection criterion, our sample was drawn from a subpopulation that is particularly resistant to desensitization.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation of the sample selection.

claim: The selection criterion did not result in particularly high levels of trait empathy in the sample.
source: An exploratory analysis provided strong evidence that our selection criterion did not result in particularly high levels of trait empathy in our sample, though.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the post hoc analysis comparing trait empathy levels.

claim: The study cannot preclude that the sample was particularly resistant to violent video game effects due to other, untested characteristics.
source: However, we cannot preclude that our sample was particularly resistant to VVG effects due to other, untested characteristics.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: To maximize the amount of violence that participants would be exposed to in the game, the game's objective was restricted to killing other characters, and this behavior was incentivized with monetary rewards.
source: To maximize the amount of violence that participants would be exposed to (and commit) in the game, we restricted the game's objective to killing other characters, and incentivized this behavior with monetary rewards.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: Restricting the game's objective to killing and incentivizing this behavior might have reduced the ecological validity of the operationalization of gaming.
source: This might have reduced the ecological validity of our operationalization of gaming, and it is possible that bigger effects could be seen when violent gameplay is more internally motivated, i.e., individuals who want to play the game may be differently affected than those that have merely accepted to be part of an experiment.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation of the study design.

claim: The results provide valid evidence that the mere exposure to virtual violence for 7 hours over 2 weeks is not sufficient to decrease empathy.
source: Still, our results provide valid evidence that the mere exposure to virtual violence for 7 hr over 2 weeks is not sufficient to decrease empathy.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about what the study does demonstrate.

claim: There are few studies that connect laboratory-based experimental investigations of empathy and emotional reactivity to real-world behavior and its measures.
source: It should be noted that there are few studies that connect laboratory-based experimental investigations of empathy and emotional reactivity to real-world behavior and its measures.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a general limitation in the field.

claim: Neuroscientific empathy measures similar to those used in the study predict individual social behavior such as donation, helping, or care-based behavior.
source: There are indications, however, that neuroscientifc empathy measures similar to the ones used here predict individual social behavior (e.g. donation, helping, or care-based behavior; Ashar et al., 2017; Hartmann et al., 2022; Hein et al., 2010; Tomova et al., 2017), and that they are also validated by their predictivity of mental or preclinical disorders characterized by deficits in empathy (Bird et al., 2010; Lamm et al., 2016, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Neuroscientific empathy measures are validated by their predictivity of mental or preclinical disorders characterized by deficits in empathy.
source: There are indications, however, that neuroscientifc empathy measures similar to the ones used here predict individual social behavior (e.g. donation, helping, or care-based behavior; Ashar et al., 2017; Hartmann et al., 2022; Hein et al., 2010; Tomova et al., 2017), and that they are also validated by their predictivity of mental or preclinical disorders characterized by deficits in empathy (Bird et al., 2010; Lamm et al., 2016, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bird et al., 2010 and Lamm et al., 2016.

claim: The empathy for pain paradigm and associated behavioral and neural responses have been shown to be malleable by external factors in previous research.
source: This argument however would contradict a wealth of findings illustrating malleability of empathic responses using this and related designs, including with placebo analgesia (Rütgen et al., 2021; Rütgen et al., 2015a; Rütgen et al., 2015b), an intervention that usually shows low to moderate effect sizes as well (see e.g. Hein and Singer, 2008; Jauniaux et al., 2019; Lamm et al., 2019, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing malleability of empathic responses.

claim: The test-retest reliability of neural covariates of empathy for pain were close to zero for all investigated regions of interest.
source: Lastly, and somewhat surprisingly, we found that the test-retest reliability of our neural covariates of empathy for pain were close to zero for all investigated ROIs.
evidence: This is a summary of the test-retest reliability results.

claim: Knowing that an individual's neural empathic response was above or below average in the first session provides little to no information about their relative response in the second session.
source: Knowing that an individual's neural empathic response (blood oxygen level-dependent [BOLD] activity for seeing somebody else in pain vs. in no pain) was above or below average in the first session provides little to no information about their relative response in the second session.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the low test-retest reliability results.

claim: To the best of the authors' knowledge, the study was the first one to present the empathy for pain paradigm to the same sample of participants after a longer time frame.
source: To the best of our knowledge, our study was the first one to present the empathy for pain paradigm to the same sample of participants after a longer time frame.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study design.

claim: The surprising result about low test-retest reliability provides valuable information on the limitations of the empathy for pain task and the neural measurements acquired in it.
source: Thus, this surprising result provides valuable information on the limitations of this task respectively the neural measurements acquired in it, and certainly demands further research to investigate the factors influencing fMRI reliability (see also Elliott et al., 2020; Kragel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the test-retest reliability findings, with citations to related work.

claim: A high test-retest reliability is not a precondition for the valid testing of group-level effects.
source: We would like to emphasize, though, that a high test-retest reliability is not a precondition for the valid testing of group-level effects.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical methodology.

claim: For a group-level effect to be testable, it is only necessary that the mean of the dependent variable is consistently affected by the independent variable.
source: For a group-level effect to be testable, it is only necessary that the mean of the dependent variable is consistently affected by the independent variable.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical methodology.

claim: Highly robust cognitive tasks are bound to exhibit low test-retest reliability, as robust tasks are often characterized by low interindividual variation.
source: Indeed, it has recently been discussed that highly robust cognitive tasks are bound to exhibit low test-retest reliability, as robust tasks are often characterized by low interindividual variation, and thus leave only little variance that can be explained by participant traits (Hedge et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hedge et al., 2018.

claim: Low reliability leads to lower power of repeated measures designs.
source: However, it must also be noted that low reliability does lead to lower power of repeated measures designs.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical methodology.

claim: The low reliability of the measured neural responses has resulted in suboptimal power of the tests on fMRI data.
source: As discussed above, the low reliability of the measured neural responses has resulted in suboptimal power of our tests on fMRI data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the test-retest reliability results and the Bayesian design analysis.

claim: The findings stand in contrast to claims that posit the playing of violent games as an essential factor for explaining decreases in empathy.
source: In summary, our findings stand in contrast to claims that posit the playing of violent games as an essential factor for explaining decreases in empathy.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: If the findings generalize to when people play more often and over longer periods, the desensitization to violence described in prior reports using quasi-experimental designs might have been caused by third and pre-existing factors.
source: If this is shown to generalize to when people play more often and over longer periods, the desensitization to violence described in prior reports using quasi-experimental designs might have been caused by third and pre-existing factors, such as education, socio-economic status, or mental health issues (DeCamp and Ferguson, 2017; Lemmens et al., 2006; Shao and Wang, 2019; Tortolero et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative explanations for previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: Together with similar findings, the results point out the limits to which violent video games can be held responsible for lacks of empathy, at least in highly controlled experimental settings that last for the 2 weeks of play implemented in the study.
source: Together with similar findings (Kühn et al., 2018), our results point out the limits to which VVGs can be held responsible for lacks of empathy, at least in highly controlled experimental settings that last for the 2 weeks of play implemented here.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the implications of the findings, with a citation to Kühn et al., 2018.

claim: The design and analysis approach of the present study could act as a reference for how future studies should be conducted to increase the stringency and robustness of research in this domain.
source: We propose that the design and analysis approach of the present study could act a reference of how future studies should be conducted, in order to increase the stringency and robustness of research in this domain.
evidence: This is a proposal about the methodological contributions of the study.

claim: The sample size of 90 participants was derived from a power analysis based on violent video game effect sizes reported in the meta-analysis of Anderson et al., 2010.
source: We planned to collect data from 90 participants. We derived this sample size from a power analysis based on VVG effect sizes reported in the meta-analysis of Anderson et al., 2010.
evidence: This is a description of the sample size determination, with a citation to Anderson et al., 2010.

claim: Anderson et al., 2010 estimated the size of the negative violent video game effect on empathy/desensitization to be r=0.194, 95% CI = [0.170, 0.217], which corresponds to Cohen's d=0.396, 95% CI = [0.345, 0.445].
source: The authors estimated the size of the negative VVG effect on empathy/desensitization to be r=0.194, 95% CI = [0.170, 0.217], which corresponds to Cohen's d=0.396, 95% CI = [0.345, 0.445], representing a small-to-medium effect.
evidence: This is a citation of effect size estimates from Anderson et al., 2010.

claim: The minimum effect size for which a power of 0.80 was desired was chosen as d=0.300 to ensure sufficient power even if the reported effect size was overestimated.
source: We chose d=0.300 as the minimum effect size for which we wanted to achieve a power of 0.80, to ensure that we would have enough power even if the reported effect size was overestimated.
evidence: This is a description of the power analysis parameters.

claim: In total, 97 participants completed the first experimental session.
source: In total, 97 participants completed the first experimental session.
evidence: This is a description of the sample.

claim: Eight participants dropped out of the study.
source: Of these, eight participants dropped out of the study (six before the first video game sessions; two after, of which one was from the experimental group and one from the control group).
evidence: This is a description of participant attrition.

claim: Complete datasets were acquired from 89 participants.
source: We thus acquired complete datasets from 89 participants.
evidence: This is a description of the final sample size.

claim: Only individuals who had not played violent video games at least 12 months before testing and had not played Grand Theft Auto V before were included.
source: To control for previous VVG exposure, we only included individuals that had not played VVGs at least 12 months before testing, and had not played the video game Grand Theft Auto V before.
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criteria.

claim: Only male participants were tested because more males than females play violent video games regularly.
source: We tested only male participants, as more males than females play VVGs regularly (Gentile et al., 2004; Krahé and Möller, 2004; Padilla-Walker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a justification for the sample selection, supported by citations.

claim: Males have been shown to be more easily influenced by violent media.
source: Moreover, males have been shown to be more easily influenced by violent media (Bartholow and Anderson, 2002; Bettencourt and Kernahan, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bartholow and Anderson, 2002 and Bettencourt and Kernahan, 1997.

claim: The age range of possible participants was restricted to 18–35 years to increase homogeneity of the sample.
source: To further increase homogeneity of the sample, we restricted the age range of possible participants to 18–35 years.
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criteria.

claim: Participants received a financial compensation of €145 for participating in all experimental sessions.
source: Participants were recruited through online advertisements and received a financial compensation of €145 for participating in all experimental sessions.
evidence: This is a description of participant compensation.

claim: A performance-linked bonus of up to €35 acted as an additional incentive during the game sessions.
source: A performance-linked bonus of up to €35 acted as an additional incentive during the game sessions.
evidence: This is a description of participant compensation.

claim: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Medical University of Vienna (decision number 1258/2017).
source: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Medical University of Vienna (decision number 1258/2017).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Participants were randomly assigned to the violent game group or the control game group.
source: Participants were randomly assigned to the violent game group or the control game group.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants completed the experimental session together with a male confederate to facilitate empathic responses during the experimental tasks.
source: To facilitate empathic responses during the experimental tasks, participants completed the experimental session together with a male confederate.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The confederate acted as if he were a second participant of the experiment.
source: The confederate acted as if he were a second participant of the experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The deception about the confederate was maintained until the end of the last experimental session, at which point participants were debriefed.
source: This deception was maintained until the end of the last experimental session, at which point participants were debriefed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Electrical stimuli were produced by a Digitimer DS5 stimulator and delivered by electrodes placed on the dorsum of the left hand.
source: Electrical stimuli were produced by a Digitimer DS5 stimulator (Digitimer Ltd, Clinical & Biomedical Research Instruments, United Kingdom) and delivered by electrodes placed on the dorsum of the left hand.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental equipment and procedure.

claim: Subjective pain thresholds were determined using a standardized calibration procedure.
source: Subjective pain thresholds were determined using a standardized calibration procedure.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The empathy-for-pain paradigm is a well-established paradigm to measure participants' empathic responses.
source: We used a well-established paradigm to measure participants' empathic responses (Hartmann et al., 2021; Rütgen et al., 2015a; Rütgen et al., 2015b; Singer et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies using this paradigm.

claim: In the empathy-for-pain task, there were 64 trials in total, with 16 trials per condition.
source: In total, there were 64 trials, with 16 trials per condition (Self Pain, Self No Pain, Other Pain, Other No Pain).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The empathy-for-pain task had a total duration of approximately 20 minutes.
source: The total task duration was approx. 20 min.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Real pictures in the emotional reactivity task were taken from the International Affective Pictures System.
source: Real pictures were taken from the International Affective Pictures System (IAPS; Lang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus materials, with a citation to Lang et al., 2005.

claim: Game pictures in the emotional reactivity task were matched to International Affective Pictures System pictures in terms of content, valence, and arousal.
source: Game pictures were matched to IAPS pictures in terms of content, valence, and arousal (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus materials.

claim: In the emotional reactivity task, participants saw 16 blocks of pictures in total, with 4 blocks per condition.
source: In total, participants saw 16 blocks of pictures, with 4 blocks per condition (Neutral Real, Neutral Game, Violent Real, Violent Game).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The emotional reactivity task had a total duration of approximately 5 minutes.
source: total task duration was approx. 5 min.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants completed the emotional reactivity task only in the second fMRI session to avoid that participants formed expectations about the purpose of the study early on.
source: To avoid that participants formed expectations about the purpose of the study early on, participants completed this task only in the second fMRI session.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: MRI data were acquired with a 3T Siemens Skyra MRI system and a 32-channel head coil.
source: MRI data were acquired with a 3T Siemens Skyra MRI system (Siemens Medical, Erlangen, Germany) and a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: This is a description of the MRI equipment.

claim: Between the two fMRI sessions, participants came seven times to the laboratory to play a video game for 1 hour.
source: Between the two fMRI sessions, participants came seven times to the laboratory to play a video game for 1 hr.
evidence: This is a description of the gaming intervention.

claim: Intervals between subsequent gaming sessions were approximately 24–48 hours.
source: Intervals between subsequent gaming sessions were approximately 24–48 hr, and the second fMRI session was completed at least 24 hr after the last gaming session.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timeline.

claim: The second fMRI session was completed at least 24 hours after the last gaming session.
source: Intervals between subsequent gaming sessions were approximately 24–48 hr, and the second fMRI session was completed at least 24 hr after the last gaming session.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timeline.

claim: Participants of both groups played a modified version of the game Grand Theft Auto V.
source: Participants of both groups played a modified version of the game Grand Theft Auto V.
evidence: This is a description of the gaming intervention.

claim: In the violent game group, participants controlled a male character equipped with a close-combat weapon.
source: In the violent game group, participants controlled a male character equipped with a close-combat weapon, and were tasked to kill as many other characters as possible.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental condition.

claim: In the violent game group, killing was graphically violent, accompanied by the splattering of blood, realistic animations of injury, and screams.
source: Killing was graphically violent, as hitting a character was accompanied by the splattering of blood, realistic animations of injury, and screams.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental condition.

claim: In the control game group, the player character had no weapon and could not hurt other characters in any way.
source: The player character had no weapon, and could not hurt other characters in any way.
evidence: This is a description of the control condition.

claim: In the control game group, the player could not be attacked by other characters, and there was no violence between non-player characters.
source: They could also not be attacked by other characters, and there was no violence between non-player characters.
evidence: This is a description of the control condition.

claim: In both groups, participants could freely explore the world of the game.
source: In both groups, participants could also freely explore the world of the game.
evidence: This is a description of the gaming intervention.

claim: Each kill or photograph was rewarded with one point, and for every two points, participants were paid out +0.01€ at the end of the study.
source: To incentivize a high number of violent or non-violent acts, each kill or photograph was rewarded with one point. For every two points, participants were paid out +0.01€ at the end of the study.
evidence: This is a description of the incentive structure.

claim: The regimen of seven 1-hourly sessions over 2 weeks was chosen as a substantial yet still feasible amount of exposure.
source: We chose our regimen (seven 1-hourly sessions over 2 weeks) as we considered this a substantial yet still feasible amount of exposure.
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental design.

claim: Number of sessions, playing time per session, and total playing time were considerably higher than in previous studies reporting violent video game effects on empathy.
source: Number of sessions, playing time per session, and total playing time were considerably higher than in previous studies reporting VVG effects on empathy (Arriaga et al., 2011; Carnagey et al., 2007; Engelhardt et al., 2011; Hasan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Preprocessing and analysis of fMRI data were performed using SPM12 implemented in MATLAB 2017b.
source: Preprocessing and analysis of fMRI data were performed using SPM12 (Wellcome Trust Centre for Neuroimaging, https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm) implemented in MATLAB 2017b.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis software.

claim: Functional images were subjected to an independent-component-analysis based algorithm for automatic removal of motion artifacts.
source: To remove motion-related artifacts, the functional images were then subjected to an independent-component-analysis based algorithm for automatic removal of motion artifacts (Pruim et al., 2015a; Pruim et al., 2015b), implemented using the FMRIB software library (FSL v5.0; http://www.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl).
evidence: This is a description of the preprocessing procedure, with citations to Pruim et al., 2015a and Pruim et al., 2015b.

claim: The aim of the masking procedure was to restrict analyses to those parts of the brain areas that are actually recruited by the task.
source: The aim of this masking procedure was to restrict analyses to those parts of the brain areas that are actually recruited by the task.
evidence: This is a description of the rationale for the analysis approach.

claim: Restricting analyses to brain areas recruited by the task increases the sensitivity of the analyses by removing signals from voxels not actually recruited by the task.
source: We believe that this increases the sensitivity of our analyses, as we remove signals from voxels that are also part of these anatomical regions, but not actually recruited by the task.
evidence: This is a justification for the analysis approach.
